questions.q: What is a SIEM correlation rule, in the terms this lesson uses?
options: Logic that fires on a specific combination or sequence of events, often across log sources, within a time window
A pattern matched against a single packet or payload the instant it's seen
A fixed list of IP addresses a SIEM blocks automatically
A dashboard widget that displays raw log counts
questions.explain: A correlation rule reasons across multiple events and time, not any one event in isolation.

questions.q: In the "5 failed logins, then 1 success, within 10 minutes" example, why does the time window matter?
options: Without it, the same failures spread across a long period would be unremarkable typos instead of a meaningful pattern
The time window only affects how the alert is displayed on a dashboard
SIEMs require a time window purely for storage efficiency, not detection logic
Time windows are optional and rarely included in real correlation rules
questions.explain: The time window is what turns a raw count into a meaningful pattern — it bounds how close together the events must occur.

questions.q: What is the real difference between a correlation rule and a network IDS signature like the ones covered in Lesson 7?
options: A signature matches a single packet/payload pattern in isolation; a correlation rule reasons across multiple events and time, often across log sources
There is no real difference — they are two names for the same mechanism
A signature only works on encrypted traffic, while a correlation rule only works on plaintext traffic
A correlation rule can only be written for firewall logs, while a signature can be written for any log source
questions.explain: A signature answers whether one thing looks malicious; a correlation rule answers whether a sequence of events adds up to something malicious.

questions.q: In the five-piece shape of a correlation rule, what does the "threshold" control?
options: How many matching events (or what sequence) are required before the rule fires
Which log source the rule reads from
The human-readable description shown in the alert
The unique numeric ID assigned to the rule
questions.explain: The threshold/sequence piece is what decides how many occurrences, or what order, trips the rule.

questions.q: Which scenario would a correlation rule catch that a single-event alert on "logon failure" alone would miss?
options: Five failed logons for the same account followed by one success, all within 10 minutes
One failed logon from an unfamiliar IP address
A single successful logon during business hours
A firewall rule blocking one inbound packet
questions.explain: No single event in that sequence is alarming on its own — it's the pattern across time that a correlation rule is built to catch.
